claim: Microglial calcium signaling has been frequently described in situ, with limited studies performed in vivo.
source: Microglial calcium activity has been frequently described in situ, with limited studies performed in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The GCaMP6s sensor was chosen for its ideal signal-to-noise ratio.
source: The GCaMP6s sensor was chosen for its ideal signal-to-noise ratio
evidence: This is a methodological choice stated by the authors based on known properties of the sensor.

claim: The Lck-GCaMP6f sensor was chosen to detect potential fast calcium transients, or transients highly localized to fine processes, as demonstrated in astrocytes (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
source: the Lck-GCaMP6f sensor was chosen to detect potential fast calcium transients, or transients highly localized to fine processes, as demonstrated in astrocytes (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: This methodological choice is supported by a citation to prior work in astrocytes.

claim: Both GCaMP6s and Lck-GCaMP6f sensors were targeted to microglia using the CX3CR1CreER-IRES-eYFP mouse line.
source: Both sensors were targeted to microglia using the CX3CR1CreER-IRES-eYFP mouse line.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: The low-level, but constitutive eYFP signal from the CX3CR1CreER-IRES-eYFP mouse was detected alongside the dynamic GCaMP6 calcium signal.
source: It is important to note that the low-level, but constitutive eYFP signal from this mouse was detected alongside the dynamic GCaMP6 calcium signal.
evidence: This is an observation made during the experiments.

claim: Spontaneous calcium activity was studied in the awake, head-restrained animal using two-photon microscopy to assess microglia in layer I and II/III of somatosensory cortex.
source: Spontaneous calcium activity was studied in the awake, head-restrained animal (Figure 1A), using two-photon microscopy to assess microglia in layer I and II/III of somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and methodology.

claim: Microglial calcium activity was present in both the Lck-GCaMP6f mouse and the cytosolic GCaMP6s mouse.
source: Microglial calcium activity was present in both the Lck-GCaMP6f mouse and the cytosolic GCaMP6s mouse (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The higher fluorescence amplitude and slower decay kinetics in the GCaMP6s animal made this fluorophore ideal for studying calcium activity in thin microglial processes.
source: However, the higher fluorescence amplitude and slower decay kinetics in the GCaMP6s animal made this fluorophore ideal for studying calcium activity in thin microglial processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed properties of the sensor.

claim: On average, GCaMP6s reported calcium transients with a 50% greater amplitude and a 60% increase in signal area compared to Lck-GCaMP6f.
source: On average, GCaMP6s reported calcium transients with a 50% greater amplitude and a 60% increase in signal area (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Calcium events were detected in a greater percentage of microdomains in the GCaMP6s animal compared to Lck-GCaMP6f.
source: For these reasons, we could detect calcium events in a greater percentage of microdomains in the GCaMP6s animal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GCaMP6s mice were adopted for studies of microglial calcium activity.
source: Therefore, we adopted GCaMP6s mice for our studies of microglial calcium activity.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the comparative data.

claim: Lck-GCaMP6f mice report small amplitude, widespread, and temporally coordinated calcium events in the parenchyma using a grid-based analysis.
source: Specifically, small amplitude, widespread, and temporally coordinated calcium events can be observed in the parenchyma of Lck-GCaMP6f mice using a grid-based analysis (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Microglia respond to a variety of stimuli, including injury and inflammation.
source: Notably, as immune cells, microglia respond to a variety of stimuli, including injury and inflammation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microglial function.

claim: The morphology of cortical microglia was highly similar in acute and chronic window studies.
source: The morphology of cortical microglia was highly similar in acute and chronic window studies (Sholl analysis, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Microglial process calcium activity was significantly greater in acute window preparations compared to chronic window preparations.
source: Despite the similarities in morphology, microglial process calcium activity was significantly greater in acute window preparations
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Microglial somatic calcium activity levels were indistinguishable between acute and chronic window preparations.
source: while somatic calcium activity levels were indistinguishable (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C-G.

claim: Approximately one-third of microglia somata exhibited calcium activity in layer I (55–75 µm depth) and layer II/III (150–170 µm depth) in both the acute and chronic window preparations.
source: Approximately one-third of microglia somata exhibited calcium activity in layer I (55–75 µm depth) and layer II/III (150–170 µm depth) in both the acute and chronic window preparations (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: In the acute window preparation, most microglia were either completely inactive (24% of cells surveyed) or had spontaneous activity in under half of their processes (40% of cells surveyed).
source: In the acute window preparation, most microglia were either completely inactive (24% of cells surveyed) or had spontaneous activity in under half of their processes (40% of cells surveyed; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: One month after surgical recovery, the proportion of active processes dropped for both layer I microglia (56% to 35%) and layer II/III microglia (54% to 41%).
source: However, one month after surgical recovery, the proportion of active processes dropped further for both layer I microglia (56% to 35%), and layer II/III microglia (54% to 41%, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Highly active processes sporadically observed across microglia in the acute window preparation were not maintained in the chronic window animal.
source: Additionally, highly active processes sporadically observed across microglia in the acute window preparation were not maintained in the chronic window animal (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an observation supported by data in Figure 2G.

claim: In the chronic window animal, baseline recordings from the same region were stable over 3 successive days of recording.
source: Notably, in the chronic window animal, baseline recordings from the same region were stable over 3 successive days of recording (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2H.

claim: All other studies were performed in chronic window mice to avoid any potential confounds associated with post-surgery microglial activation (Xu et al., 2007).
source: For these reasons, we performed all other studies in chronic window mice to avoid any potential confounds associated with post-surgery microglial activation (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The isoflurane concentration chosen for maintenance (1.5–2% in oxygen) is intended to mimic strong sensory blockade during surgery and is higher than the concentration typically used during anesthetized imaging (0.5–1.5%).
source: Importantly, the isoflurane concentration chosen for maintenance (1.5–2% in oxygen) is intended to mimic strong sensory blockade during surgery and is higher than the concentration typically used during anesthetized imaging (0.5–1.5%).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design.

claim: 1.5–2% isoflurane maintenance can reduce excitatory calcium signaling by 91 ± 0.11% in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Our studies of neuronal activity indicate that 1.5–2% isoflurane maintenance can reduce excitatory calcium signaling by 91 ± 0.11% in the somatosensory cortex (AAV.CaMKIIa.GCaMP6s.WPRE transfected mice, layer II/III of somatosensory cortex; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from neuronal calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: In response to strongly reduced neuronal activity, microglia demonstrate an increase in process calcium activity.
source: In response to strongly reduced neuronal activity, microglia demonstrate an increase in process calcium activity (Figure 3E–G and Figure 3—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3E-G and Figure 3—Video 1.

claim: Increased microglial process calcium activity is first detected 6 min after anesthesia.
source: Increased microglial process calcium activity is first detected 6 min after anesthesia (Figure 3H)
evidence: This is a temporal finding supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: Microglial process calcium activity reaches peak levels approximately 10–20 min after isoflurane induction.
source: and reaches peak levels approximately 10–20 min after isoflurane induction (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a temporal finding supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: At their peak, microglial processes display a 290 ± 29% increase in average ∆F/F calcium signal area under isoflurane.
source: At their peak, microglial processes display a 290 ± 29% increase in average ∆F/F calcium signal area (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Microglial somatic calcium signaling remained unaffected under general anesthesia, with no changes in the proportion or signal area of somatic events.
source: Despite strong increases in process calcium activity, somatic calcium signaling remained unaffected in microglia under general anesthesia, with no changes in the proportion or signal area of somatic events (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Microglial compartments could have distinct calcium-associated functions.
source: These results provide early evidence that microglial compartments could have distinct calcium-associated functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential calcium responses in soma versus processes.

claim: General anesthesia increases microglial process outgrowth.
source: In accordance with our previous studies in the awake animal, general anesthesia increases microglial process outgrowth (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A gradual increase in total process area co-occurs with increased process calcium activity under isoflurane.
source: At the isoflurane concentration used, we observed a gradual increase in total process area co-occurring with increased process calcium activity (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microglia have a unique morphological response to isoflurane, characterized by extension and outgrowth of sub-branchlets from main processes.
source: In vivo, we observe that microglia have a unique morphological response to isoflurane, characterized by extension and outgrowth of sub-branchlets from main processes (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation supported by data in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Areas of new process extension/outgrowth exhibit the largest calcium signals and the highest association with calcium activity.
source: These areas of new process extension/outgrowth exhibit the largest calcium signals and the highest association with calcium activity (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Processes with little-to-no motility (termed 'stable' processes) had significantly less associated calcium activity and signal magnitude.
source: On the other hand, processes with little-to-no motility (termed 'stable' processes) had significantly less associated calcium activity and signal magnitude.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Processes that retracted during isoflurane exposure exhibited much lower associated calcium activity and signal magnitude.
source: Processes that retracted during isoflurane exposure also exhibited much lower associated calcium activity and signal magnitude (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3I.

claim: Calcium activity increases under isoflurane are most directly associated with process extension and sub-branchlet outgrowth.
source: Our observations suggest that calcium activity increases under isoflurane are most directly associated with process extension and sub-branchlet outgrowth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between motility and calcium activity.

claim: Kainate is an excitatory receptor agonist and chemoconvulsant.
source: We additionally used kainate, an excitatory receptor agonist and chemoconvulsant
evidence: This is established knowledge about kainate.

claim: A first generalized seizure began between 45 and 75 min after kainate administration.
source: A first generalized seizure began between 45 and 75 min after kainate administration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental protocol.

claim: Seizure generalization involves activation of cortical neuronal populations.
source: Seizure generalization involves activation of cortical neuronal populations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about seizure activity.

claim: Kainate increased excitatory calcium activity both soon after administration (15–30 min) and after the first observed seizure (55-fold increase in signal area).
source: In neuronal studies (AAV.CaMKIIa.GCaMP6s.WPRE transfected mice), kainate increased excitatory calcium activity both soon after administration (15–30 min) and after the first observed seizure (55-fold increase in signal area; Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from neuronal calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: After the first observed seizure, microglial process calcium activity was increased by 360 ± 26%, with a greater proportion of processes exhibiting calcium activity (32% to 73%).
source: After the first observed seizure, microglial process calcium activity was increased by 360 ± 26%, with a greater proportion of processes exhibiting calcium activity (32% to 73%; Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Microglial somatic signaling did not increase significantly as measured through average signal area after kainate-induced seizures; however, there was an increase in the proportion of somata exhibiting calcium activity (29% to 44%).
source: Despite strong increases in process calcium signaling, microglial somatic signaling did not increase significantly as measured through average signal area; however, there was an increase in the proportion of somata exhibiting calcium activity (29% to 44%; Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: During kainate-induced seizures, the predominant motility behavior was process extension, with process area increasing across the parenchyma.
source: During kainate-induced seizures, the predominant motility behavior was process extension, with process area increasing across the parenchyma (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Both an approach to rapidly decrease neuronal activity (isoflurane) and an approach to rapidly increase neuronal activity (kainate) similarly result in large-scale increases in microglial process calcium activity.
source: These findings demonstrate that both an approach to rapidly decrease neuronal activity (isoflurane) and an approach to rapidly increase neuronal activity (kainate) similarly result in large-scale increases in microglial process calcium activity.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the isoflurane and kainate experiments.

claim: Both isoflurane and kainate approaches resulted in increased microglial process territory and were insufficient to alter microglial somatic calcium activity.
source: In addition, both approaches resulted in increased microglial process territory and were insufficient to alter microglial somatic calcium activity.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the isoflurane and kainate experiments.

claim: The prolonged seizure state induced by kainate, called status epilepticus, can serve as a precipitating insult for the later acquisition of epilepsy (Puttachary et al., 2015; Tse et al., 2014; Umpierre et al., 2016).
source: The prolonged seizure state induced by kainate, called status epilepticus, can also serve as a precipitating insult for the later acquisition of epilepsy (Puttachary et al., 2015; Tse et al., 2014; Umpierre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For up to 7 days after kainate status epilepticus, layer I microglia displayed an altered morphology, marked by greater process ramification.
source: For up to 7 days after kainate status epilepticus, layer I microglia displayed an altered morphology, marked by greater process ramification (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over a 7-day time course after kainate status epilepticus, a greater proportion of microglial somata and processes displayed calcium activity, with increased calcium signaling lasting up to 10 days.
source: Over the same 7-day time course, a greater proportion of microglial somata and processes displayed calcium activity, with increased calcium signaling lasting up to 10 days (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C-E.

claim: During the period after kainate status epilepticus, microglial somata and processes could sustain high amplitude (>2 fold ∆F/F) calcium transients for exceptionally long periods (1–4 min).
source: During this period, microglial somata and processes could sustain high amplitude (>2 fold ∆F/F) calcium transients for exceptionally long periods (1–4 min; see ∆F/F traces in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Calcium activity was highly synchronized between the processes and soma after kainate status epilepticus, exemplified by the appearance of large, spreading microglial calcium waves.
source: Calcium activity was also highly synchronized between the processes and soma, best exemplified by the appearance of large, spreading microglial calcium waves (Figure 5D and Figure 5—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D and Figure 5—Video 1.

claim: The proportion of active microdomains and their signal areas are highly similar during the 14-day period after kainate status epilepticus.
source: For these reasons, it is not surprising that the proportion of active microdomains and their signal areas are highly similar during this 14-day period (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: Both somata and processes showed large increases in calcium activity before returning to near-baseline levels two weeks after kainate status epilepticus.
source: Both somata and processes showed large increases in calcium activity before returning to near-baseline levels two weeks later (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: Only after the excitotoxic insult represented by kainate status epilepticus do we observe consistent increases in microglial somatic calcium activity and the appearance of coordinated, whole-cell calcium transients.
source: Only after the excitotoxic insult represented by kainate status epilepticus do we observe consistent increases in microglial somatic calcium activity and the appearance of coordinated, whole-cell calcium transients.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the longitudinal findings after kainate status epilepticus.

claim: The appearance of increased somatic calcium activity and coordinated, whole-cell calcium transients suggest microglial calcium activity can be fundamentally changed following excitotoxicity.
source: The appearance of both phenomena suggest microglial calcium activity can be fundamentally changed following excitotoxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes after kainate status epilepticus.

claim: In the days following kainate status epilepticus, microglial processes became exceptionally motile.
source: In the days following kainate status epilepticus, microglial processes became exceptionally motile (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: One day after kainate status epilepticus, 93% of microglial processes undergoing extension exhibit calcium activity, compared to 45% of stable processes and 38% of retracting processes.
source: One day after kainate status epilepticus, we find that 93% of microglial processes undergoing extension exhibit calcium activity, compared to 45% of stable processes and 38% of retracting processes (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: Extending processes exhibit calcium signaling nearly three-times the magnitude of stable or retracting processes after kainate status epilepticus.
source: Extending processes also exhibit calcium signaling nearly three-times the magnitude of stable or retracting processes (Figure 5G and Figure 5—Video 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 5G and Figure 5—Video 2.

claim: 51% of extending processes have a closely aligned calcium event (within 60 s) after kainate status epilepticus, compared to 18% of retracting processes.
source: we find that 51% of extending processes have a closely aligned calcium event (within 60 s), compared to 18% of retracting processes (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 5H.

claim: After status epilepticus, microglial process extension is temporally correlated and strongly associated with their calcium activity.
source: Our analysis suggests that after status epilepticus, microglial process extension is temporally correlated and strongly associated with their calcium activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation analysis.

claim: DREADDs (Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs) utilize the expression of exogenous G-protein receptors to modulate cellular activity (Roth, 2016).
source: DREADDs (Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs) utilize the expression of exogenous G-protein receptors to modulate cellular activity (Roth, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DREADDs supported by citation.

claim: A Gi system (hM4D) was used to decrease neuronal activity and a Gq system (hM3D) was used to increase neuronal activity.
source: We used a Gi system (hM4D) targeted to local CaMKIIa neurons of the somatosensory cortex to decrease neuronal activity and a Gq system (hM3D) to increase neuronal activity (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: In the Gi system, a 2.5 mg/kg (i.p.) dose of CNO decreased CaMKIIa calcium signaling by 51 ± 4.2%, while a 5.0 mg/kg dose decreased signaling by 66 ± 3.5%.
source: In the Gi system, a 2.5 mg/kg (i.p.) dose of CNO decreased CaMKIIa calcium signaling by 51 ± 4.2%, while a 5.0 mg/kg dose decreased signaling by 66 ± 3.5%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the dose-response experiments.

claim: A 1.25 mg/kg (i.p.) dose of CNO in the Gi system resulted in a 31 ± 2.7% decrease in CaMKIIa calcium activity.
source: Due to the similar responses, a 1.25 mg/kg (i.p.) dose of CNO was also tested, resulting in a 31 ± 2.7% decrease in CaMKIIa calcium activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the dose-response experiments.

claim: In the Gi system, peak reductions in excitatory signaling were reached 30 min after injection and were sustained for at least 30 min thereafter.
source: In the Gi system, peak reductions in excitatory signaling were reached 30 min after injection and were sustained for at least 30 min thereafter (Figure 6B,D and E).
evidence: This is a temporal finding supported by data in Figure 6B, D, and E.

claim: In the Gq system, a 2.5 mg/kg (i.p.) dose of CNO increased excitatory neuronal calcium signaling by 42 ± 6.5%, while a 5.0 mg/kg dose increased signaling by 70 ± 8%.
source: In the Gq system, a 2.5 mg/kg (i.p.) dose of CNO increased excitatory neuronal calcium signaling by 42 ± 6.5%, while a 5.0 mg/kg dose increased signaling by 70 ± 8%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the dose-response experiments.

claim: In the Gq system, there was a clear peak effect 30–45 min after injection.
source: In the Gq system, there was a clear peak effect 30–45 min after injection (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is a temporal finding supported by data in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The highest dose of CNO used (5 mg/kg) did not alter neuronal calcium signaling in mice without DREADD transfection.
source: In a control study, the highest dose of CNO used (5 mg/kg) did not alter neuronal calcium signaling in mice without DREADD transfection (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a control experiment supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: In the Gi system, CNO-dependent decreases in CaMKIIa neuronal activity resulted in gradual increases in microglial process calcium activity, peaking 45–60 min after injection.
source: In the Gi system, CNO-dependent decreases in CaMKIIa neuronal activity resulted in gradual increases in microglial process calcium activity, peaking 45–60 min after injection (Figure 6G,I , J, and Figure 6—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6G, I, J, and Figure 6—Video 1.

claim: There were clear dose-dependent differences in the extent of microglial process calcium activity after CNO injection in the Gi system.
source: Notably, there were clear dose-dependent differences in the extent of microglial process calcium activity after CNO injection (Figure 6I and J)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6I and J.

claim: At the lower dose (1.25 mg/kg) in the Gi system, a 64 ± 11% increase in microglial process calcium activity was observed, while at the higher dose (5.0 mg/kg), a 133 ± 26% increase was observed.
source: with a 64 ± 11% increase observed at the lower dose (1.25 mg/kg) and a 133 ± 26% increase observed at the higher dose (5.0 mg/kg).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the DREADD experiments.

claim: In the Gq system, microglial process calcium activity displayed highly similar trends to the Gi system, despite opposing shifts to neuronal activity.
source: In the Gq system, microglial process calcium activity displayed highly similar trends to the Gi system, despite the fact that these approaches resulted in opposing shifts to neuronal activity (hypoactivity in the Gi system and hyperactivity in the Gq system).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the DREADD experiments.

claim: At the lower dose (2.5 mg/kg) in the Gq system, CNO administration resulted in a 68 ± 31% increase in microglial process calcium activity, while the higher dose (5.0 mg/kg) resulted in a 128 ± 13% increase.
source: At the lower dose in the Gq system, 2.5 mg/kg CNO administration resulted in a 68 ± 31% increase in microglial process calcium activity, while the higher dose (5.0 mg/kg) resulted in a 128 ± 13% increase in process calcium activity (Figure 6H–J, and Figure 6—Video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 6H-J and Figure 6—Video 1.

claim: In both the Gi and Gq systems, peak microglial calcium responses occurred 45–60 min after CNO administration, suggesting an approximate 15 min latency relative to peak neuronal changes.
source: In both the Gi and Gq systems, peak microglial calcium responses occurred 45–60 min after CNO administration, suggesting an approximate 15 min latency relative to peak neuronal changes (Figure 6D and I).
evidence: This is a temporal finding supported by data in Figure 6D and I.

claim: Both Gq- and Gi-based alterations to excitatory neuronal activity did not result in observable changes to microglial somatic calcium signaling.
source: Additionally, both Gq- and Gi-based alterations to excitatory neuronal activity did not result in observable changes to microglial somatic calcium signaling (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Microglial process extension/outgrowth was the predominant motility behavior observed following Gi- or Gq-DREADD activation in neurons.
source: Similar to isoflurane and kainate experiments, microglial process extension/outgrowth was the predominant motility behavior observed following Gi- or Gq-DREADD activation in neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Extension was the motility behavior most closely associated with calcium activity and large signal magnitude in DREADD experiments.
source: Extension was the motility behavior most closely associated with calcium activity and large signal magnitude (Figure 6K,L, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6K, L, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A near-linear range of neuronal activity shifts results in a U-shaped curve of microglial process calcium activity, with the greatest shifts in neuronal activity producing the largest microglial process calcium signaling.
source: Overall, we observe that a near-linear range of neuronal activity shifts (Figure 6E) results in a U-shaped curve of microglial process calcium activity (Figure 6J), with the greatest shifts in neuronal activity producing the largest microglial process calcium signaling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings across all experiments, supported by data in Figures 6E, 6J, and 7.

claim: Microglia are considered to have the lowest levels of spontaneous calcium activity in 'resting' or 'baseline' states from reports in anesthetized mice (Brawek et al., 2017; Eichhoff et al., 2011; Pozner et al., 2015).
source: In general, microglia are considered to have the lowest levels of spontaneous calcium activity in 'resting' or 'baseline' states from reports in anesthetized mice (Brawek et al., 2017; Eichhoff et al., 2011; Pozner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglial calcium activity is similarly low in awake, chronic window mice.
source: We observe that microglial calcium activity is similarly low in awake, chronic window mice (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Pharmacological alterations in neuronal activity can trigger microglial process calcium signaling without impacting somatic calcium signaling.
source: However, pharmacological alterations in neuronal activity can trigger microglial process calcium signaling without impacting somatic calcium signaling (Figures 3, 4 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Microglial process calcium signaling follows a U-shaped curve, with greater shifts in neuronal activity (both hypoactive or hyperactive) resulting in stronger process calcium signaling.
source: In general, microglial process calcium signaling follows a U-shaped curve, with greater shifts in neuronal activity (both hypoactive or hyperactive) resulting in stronger process calcium signaling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Both shifts in network activity (hypoactive and hyperactive) were associated with microglial process extension/outgrowth.
source: Additionally, both shifts in network activity were associated with microglial process extension/outgrowth.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings across experiments.

claim: Extending processes consistently demonstrated the greatest calcium activity.
source: Extending processes consistently demonstrated the greatest calcium activity.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings across experiments.

claim: Microglial calcium signaling may be an important component in how microglia address brain state changes.
source: Our work initially suggests that microglial calcium signaling may be an important component in how microglia address brain state changes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Microglial have low spontaneous calcium activity in the anesthetized animal (Brawek et al., 2017; Eichhoff et al., 2011; Pozner et al., 2015), relative to reports of calcium activity in neurons and astrocytes.
source: Microglial have low spontaneous calcium activity in the anesthetized animal (Brawek et al., 2017; Eichhoff et al., 2011; Pozner et al., 2015), relative to reports of calcium activity in neurons and astrocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Even in the awake animal, microglia display very infrequent spontaneous process and soma calcium activity.
source: Even in the awake animal, microglia do indeed display very infrequent spontaneous process and soma calcium activity (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Injury, damage, and inflammation all produce increased or altered microglial calcium signaling (Brawek et al., 2017; Brawek et al., 2014; Eichhoff et al., 2011; Pozner et al., 2015).
source: Previous studies also arrive on a key concept that injury, damage, and inflammation all produce increased or altered microglial calcium signaling (Brawek et al., 2017; Brawek et al., 2014; Eichhoff et al., 2011; Pozner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia can maintain a more reactive phenotype for multiple weeks after craniotomy (Xu et al., 2007).
source: By some reports, microglia can maintain a more reactive phenotype for multiple weeks after craniotomy (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Chronic window preparations may better reflect the occurrence and magnitude of true spontaneous microglial calcium activity.
source: These observations suggest that chronic window preparations may better reflect the occurrence and magnitude of true spontaneous microglial calcium activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between acute and chronic window preparations.

claim: The stability of spontaneous calcium activity in chronic window preparations over multiple days suggests that it is ideal for longitudinal studies.
source: The stability of spontaneous calcium activity in this preparation over multiple days also suggests that it is ideal for longitudinal studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability data.

claim: The coordinated, low-level signals detected by the Lck-GCaMP6f mouse could reflect neuronal activity changes sensed by surrounding microglial processes.
source: We hypothesize that the coordinated, low-level signals detected by the Lck-GCaMP6f mouse could reflect neuronal activity changes sensed by surrounding microglial processes.
